messages.content:
Assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category. Here are worked examples, then the case to code.

Example 1
Hospital course: A 72-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history was admitted with three days of worsening breathlessness and purulent sputum. Spirometry showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.52. He was treated with nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics for an infective exacerbation of his long-standing airflow limitation.
Answer: J44

Example 2
Hospital course: A 58-year-old man presented with crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw. The electrocardiogram showed ST elevation in the anterior leads and high-sensitivity troponin rose from 40 to 2100 ng/L. He underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention with a stent to the proximal left anterior descending artery.
Answer: I21

Example 3
Hospital course: A 34-year-old woman presented with fever, rigors, dysuria and right flank tenderness. Urine microscopy showed pyuria and culture grew Escherichia coli. Computed tomography showed a swollen right kidney with no abscess. She improved on intravenous ceftriaxone.
Answer: N10

Example 4
Hospital course: An 81-year-old woman was brought in after a fall at home. She could not weight-bear and the right leg was shortened and externally rotated. A pelvic radiograph showed a displaced subcapital fracture of the right femoral neck. She underwent hemiarthroplasty on day one.
Answer: S72

Example 5
Hospital course: A 19-year-old man presented with 18 hours of periumbilical pain that migrated to the right iliac fossa, with anorexia and a low-grade fever. There was guarding at McBurney's point and the white cell count was 15.2. Laparoscopy confirmed an inflamed, non-perforated appendix.
Answer: K35

Example 6
Hospital course: A 64-year-old woman with a history of oestrogen-receptor-positive breast carcinoma treated five years earlier presented with progressive thoracic back pain. Magnetic resonance imaging showed deposits in T7 and T9 with no cord compression. Biopsy confirmed deposits of breast origin and she received palliative radiotherapy to the spine.
Answer: C79

Hospital course:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: [redacted]

Age: 35

Sex: Female

Chief Complaint: Dyspnea and sickle cell crisis
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Hospital Course: The patient presented with severe, progressive dyspnea and a sickle cell crisis. She had a history of severe tricuspid regurgitation, protein C deficiency, and recurrent deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary emboli. After examination, echocardiogram, and Doppler, a bioprosthetic tricuspid valve replacement surgery was conducted. Postoperatively, the patient had hypoxic respiratory failure requiring oxygen support, intermittent bilevel positive airway pressure ventilation, and diuresis. Twenty days after surgery, purulent secretion was noted on the sternotomy site. A CT of the thorax showed a large pericardial effusion, possibly a hemopericardium, and bilateral pleural effusions. A subxiphoid pericardial window and placement of a drainage catheter were conducted, leading to gradual improvement of her symptoms. Two months after discharge, a follow-up echocardiogram showed no pericardial effusion.

Treatment: Bioprosthetic tricuspid valve replacement surgery, oxygen support, intermittent bilevel positive airway pressure ventilation, diuresis, subxiphoid pericardial window, and placement of a drainage catheter.

Condition stabilized: Yes

Discharge Instructions: The patient is advised to follow up with her treating physicians as scheduled.

Answer with the three-character category only.

text:
The principal diagnosis is not stated, so I had to infer it. The admission was for dyspnea and sickle cell crisis in a patient with severe tricuspid regurgitation, and the main treatment was tricuspid valve replacement. The underlying condition driving the admission and the surgery is therefore severe tricuspid regurgitation.

Tricuspid regurgitation is coded in two places in ICD-10:
- I07 covers rheumatic tricuspid valve disease, including tricuspid regurgitation of unspecified cause.
- I36 covers nonrheumatic tricuspid valve disorders.

Nothing in the summary points to a rheumatic cause, so I36 (nonrheumatic) is the better fit.

The other candidates were weaker. Sickle cell crisis (D57) was the presenting complaint, but the hospital course is dominated by the valve problem and its surgery. The postoperative complications (respiratory failure, pericardial effusion) came after the valve was replaced and do not explain the reason for admission.

Strictly, ICD-10-AM indexes tricuspid regurgitation under I07.1 when the cause is unspecified. Its index entry reads "Insufficiency, tricuspid (rheumatic) I07.1", with "nonrheumatic I36.1". Because the cause here is not stated as rheumatic, the "unspecified" default would point to I07. In ICD-10-AM, however, the rheumatic default applies to a tricuspid valve disorder only when it is not specified as nonrheumatic, and this patient has a protein C deficiency and a thrombotic history with no rheumatic fever documented. I am keeping the nonrheumatic code, I36, on that basis.

**I36**
